title: Karna bows to his father
hookLine: crowned a king in the arena, Karna bows to the old charioteer who raised him, and pays for it with an insult
carry: pitru devo bhava: honor the one who raised you
tomorrow: why send the Pandavas on holiday?

lines: A PRINCE FIGHTS ONLY AN EQUAL.
cards: Two fighters are ready to face each other. Then Kripa, one of the teachers, steps between them with a question that sounds polite. Arjuna is a prince, son of Pandu and Kunti.
Tell us your mother and father, your royal line. A prince fights only an equal. And Karna, who has just matched every feat in the arena, has no answer to give.
The text says he lowers his face.

teach.h: DURYODHANA CROWNS HIM KING OF ANGA.
teach.b: Duryodhana jumps in. If Arjuna will only fight a king, then let Karna be a king. And there in the arena he has Karna crowned king of Anga.
Karna, overwhelmed, asks what he can give in return. Duryodhana asks only for his friendship, and Karna gives it. Then, through the crowd, comes an old man, trembling, his cloth slipping.
It's Adhiratha, the charioteer who pulled a basket from the river.
And Karna, the new king, his hair still wet from the crowning, bows his head to him and greets him as his father. Adhiratha holds him and weeps. It's the moment Bhima has been waiting for.

You're a charioteer's son, he says, so pick up a whip; you're not fit to fight Arjuna, or to rule Anga. Duryodhana defends his friend: the origins of heroes, like the sources of rivers, are hard to know.
Then the sun sets, and the day ends with nothing settled. Now go back to that bow. Hindus have an old teaching for it.
In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends his students home with these words: let your mother be a god to you, let your father be a god to you, your teacher, and your guest.
Matru devo bhava, pitru devo bhava.

teach.h: HONOR THE ONE WHO RAISED YOU.
teach.b: It's why Hindu children still bend to touch the feet of parents and elders, at festivals, before exams, before a big day, and receive a hand on the head and a blessing. Karna could have pretended not to know the old man.
Everyone was watching. He bowed instead, and paid for it with an insult.

how: Hindu children still touch the feet of parents and elders, at festivals, before exams and big days, and receive a blessing; retellings often point to Karna's bow to Adhiratha as that honor given in front of a whole city.

o: a prince who gives up his crown to stay a charioteer
a charioteer's son who defeats Arjuna in the arena
a king crowned and mocked on the same afternoon

games.q: the afternoon in the arena — tap the pairs.
p: let your father be a god to you

s: Karna refused to acknowledge Adhiratha in front of the crowd
newly crowned, he bowed his head to the old charioteer and greeted him as his father.
Duryodhana asked for Karna's friendship in return for Anga
Karna asked what he could give, and Duryodhana asked only for friendship.
touching an elder's feet is a sign of fear
it's honor: a bow to someone the Upanishad says to treat as a god, and they answer with a blessing.

games.q: you're Karna, just crowned king. an old charioteer, trembling, comes through the crowd toward you. everyone is watching. what do you do?
o: bow your head and greet him as your father.
send a servant to lead him away.
games.why: he bows to Adhiratha with his hair still wet from the crowning: pitru devo bhava, in front of everyone. it's the moment Bhima uses to mock him.

practice: If a parent, grandparent or elder is near today, try the old greeting: bend and touch their feet, or bow with joined hands, and let them bless you.
If no one's near, picture the one who raised you, the way Karna saw Adhiratha coming through the crowd, and bow to them in your mind. If you don't pray, a call or a message of thanks is the same bow.

wordCard.voice: Karna's abandonment. Asked his lineage, he lowers his face; crowned king, he bows to the charioteer who raised him; and the secret of his birth goes on following him.

orig.note: Sanskrit praṇāma: a bow of respect; touching an elder's feet is one form.

carryVoice: Your line: pitru devo bhava, honor the one who raised you. A new king bowed to a charioteer. Tomorrow: why send the Pandavas on holiday?

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Kripa asks Karna's lineage; Karna made king of Anga; Adhiratha enters; Bhima's taunt; Duryodhana's reply; sunset ends the day)
Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.2 (the teacher's parting words: let your mother, father, teacher and guest be gods to you)
Touching the feet of parents and elders (pranam, charan sparsh), common Hindu practice, in general
